Starling Bank Scam UK: Spot a Fake Fraud Alert

Starling Bank scammers are after your login details and security codes—here's exactly how to spot them before you lose money.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-05-18 · Updated 2026-08-01 · 6 min read

Quick answer: Starling will never ask you to make or approve payments to keep your account safe, so any 'move your money' contact is a scam. Check alerts in the Starling app itself, use its Call Status feature to verify callers, and call 159 if a payment request feels suspicious.
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

What a Starling scam looks like

A Starling scam impersonates Starling Bank, or a caller claiming to be from its fraud team, to get you to move money, share your login, or read out a one-time code. Because Starling is app-only, a common trick is a call or message claiming your account is "compromised" and that you must act immediately to protect it. An example of the style is: Starling: We've detected suspicious activity on your account. Verify your identity now or your account will be suspended: starling-verify.example.

This guide shows the warning signs, how to check safely, and what to do if you have already responded.

Why these scams are convincing

Starling has no branches, so customers are used to managing the account digitally and receiving support through the app, phone or message. That familiarity can make an impersonator's contact feel plausible. A spoofed number and a caller who already knows your name or part of your account details do the rest.

Starling built its answer into the app. The call status indicator, introduced in 2024, tells you which of a handful of states applies — including "We've never called you" and "You're on a call with Starling" — and it sits on the home screen and the payment screen, so it is in front of you exactly when a caller is pressing you to send money. Starling says it will never ask you to make or approve payments to keep your account safe, and that no bank would ask for your full card number or PIN.

Signs a Starling message is a scam

  • It claims suspicious activity or a compromised account and demands immediate action.
  • It asks you to "verify" through a link, or to confirm your PIN, password, or a one-time code.
  • You are told to move money to a new, "safe", or "holding" account.
  • A caller claims to be from Starling's fraud team and pressures you to stay on the line.
  • The link is not starlingbank.com or inside the genuine Starling app.
  • You are asked to install screen-sharing software during the call. TSB customers see the same approach by text, including screenshots sent to a reporting inbox — our TSB scam text guide covers it.

How the scam works

The sequence keeps you inside the Starling app while working against your own interests. It opens with an unexpected call, text or email about "suspicious activity". It escalates: a payment is supposedly leaving your account now, and only an immediate transfer will stop it. Then comes the destination — a "safe account" read out to you, or a new payee you are talked through adding.

Because you tap the buttons yourself, the payment counts as authorised, which is why criminals want it done this way rather than stealing a card. "Authorised" describes how the payment was initiated; it does not automatically mean the customer is ineligible under the mandatory APP reimbursement rules.

The pressure is designed to prevent you checking independently, including reading the Call Status on the payment screen. Checking anyway, and declining to move money on the strength of a phone call, ends the attempt.

How to check a Starling alert safely

If anything feels rushed, stop.

  • Open the Starling app directly and check your transactions and account status there.
  • Use the Starling app's Call Status feature to check whether Starling is calling you. If it does not show Starling is calling, hang up.
  • Know its limits: Starling says a genuine call may not display correctly if your app is out of date or there is no internet connection. Do not continue the call on that basis — reconnect, or hang up and dial 159.
  • Use in-app chat, or Starling's official fraud number published on starlingbank.com, if you need help, and call 159 if a payment request feels suspicious.
  • Never move money to a "safe", "holding", or "protected" account; Starling will not ask you to.
  • Never share a one-time code, your PIN, or your full password to anyone.
  • Do not install remote-access or screen-sharing software during an unexpected call.

If you are unsure whether a linked page is genuine, our guide on Is This Website a Scam? A Practical Checklist Before You Buy helps, and our Monzo Scam UK: Spot a Fake 'Suspicious Activity' Alert guide covers the same pattern with another app-based bank.

If you responded or shared details

Act now using the payment, account and identity steps in our scam recovery checklist.

How to report a Starling scam (UK)

Report it to Starling through in-app chat or the official fraud number published on starlingbank.com. If a payment request feels wrong mid-call, hang up and dial 159 instead — Starling is one of the participating banks, so the call goes out on a line you chose rather than one the caller controls. Scam texts can be forwarded to 7726; phishing emails go to report@phishing.gov.uk.

Where money has gone or security details were shared, our scam recovery checklist sets out the police routes for each UK nation, the evidence worth keeping, and the complaint route if a claim is refused.

Frequently asked questions

Is Starling safe, or are these alerts real?

Starling itself is a genuine, regulated bank. The scam is the impersonation around it. Check your account directly in the Starling app, and never trust a link or number from an unexpected call or message.

Someone says my Starling account is compromised and I must move money to a safe account — real?

No. That is always a scam. Starling will never ask you to move money to a "safe" or "holding" account. Open the app yourself and use in-app chat if you are unsure.

A caller claims to be from Starling's fraud team — how do I check?

Check the Starling app's Call Status feature. If it does not show Starling is calling, hang up and contact Starling through in-app chat, its official fraud number on starlingbank.com, or 159. If the banner does not appear at all, check whether your app is out of date or your phone is offline rather than trusting the caller's explanation. Never call a number given to you during the suspicious call, and never share a one-time code, PIN, or password.

I shared my login or moved money — can I get it back?

Maybe. Report it in the Starling app immediately, or call Starling's official fraud number on starlingbank.com, to secure your account. Eligible UK transfers since 7 October 2024 may fall under APP reimbursement rules, subject to limits and exclusions. Being told the payment was "authorised" does not by itself end a claim.

How do I report a Starling scam?

Report it through the Starling app's in-app chat or by calling its official fraud number on starlingbank.com, then if you lost money or shared details, report it to Report Fraud in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.
